title: 12V winch from a gear motor
summary: Turn a geared 12–24V motor (car wiper motor, power-seat motor, wheelchair motor) into a small electric winch for dragging logs, raising a tank or hauling a boat. A wiper motor pulls tens of kilograms; a wheelchair motor much more. Add pulleys for more pull. Never lift over people.

materials.item: Gear motor: car wiper or seat motor (12V, worm gear), wheelchair motor (24V), or ride-on toy gear motor
Extra reduction: gearbox or chain and sprockets, for more pull
Drum: steel pipe 30–60 mm across, 60–120 mm long
Drum flanges and base plate: steel plate 3–6 mm
Bearing to support the drum's outer end
Rope 6–10 mm (synthetic) or steel cable 3–5 mm, rated 5× the load
Momentary reversing switch (DPDT, centre-off) or two relays
Relays, for remote or high-current switching
Fuse and holder within 30 cm of battery +, 15–30A
Bolts, a hook or shackle, and a strap to anchor the winch

steps.text: Choose the motor. Worm-geared wiper and seat motors hold their load when stopped. Wheelchair motors are much stronger and often have a brake that holds when power is off.
Find the terminals: with a 10–15A fused lead from a 12V battery, try pairs of terminals. Wiper motors have a slow and a fast winding plus a park switch; use the slow pair. Measure running current.
steps.warn: Clamp the motor down before powering it; its output arm swings hard.

steps.text: Make the drum: weld or bolt a flange disc at each end of the pipe, tall enough to hold all the rope with 1–2 cm spare. Drill a hole to anchor the rope end.
Couple the drum to the output shaft: bolt it to the wiper's crank arm, or pin or weld it to the shaft. For loads over a few kilos, support the far end of the drum in a bearing on the base.
Bolt motor and drum to a rigid base plate. The base needs a strong anchor point to strap to a tree, post or vehicle.
Measure what it can pull: lift a bucket and add water until the motor nearly stalls. Working load is a third to a half of that.

Wire the reversing switch: motor leads to the two middle terminals; battery + to one top terminal and the opposite bottom terminal, battery − to the other two (an X). Use a momentary switch so it stops when you let go.

Fit the fuse within 30 cm of battery positive. Size it above the motor's running current under load and at or below the wire's rating: typically 15A for a wiper motor on 14 AWG, 30A for a wheelchair motor on 10 AWG.
steps.warn: Stall current can be 3–5× running current. A fuse may not blow quickly on a stall, and a stalled motor heats fast: let go of the switch if it slows hard.

steps.text: Wind on the rope neatly, keeping at least 3–5 wraps on the drum at full pay-out.
Test with small loads, then build up to the working load. Use pulley blocks for heavier pulls.
steps.warn: A snapping rope or cable whips back hard enough to maim. Stand to the side of the line, lay a heavy coat or bag over it midway, and wear gloves.

steps.text: In use: never lift over people or let anyone stand under or beside a load. Once the load is in place, tie it off with a separate rope or strap; don't leave it hanging on the motor.
steps.warn: Crush danger: chock or block loads before anyone reaches under them.

notes:
## Pull maths
Pull (N) = torque (N·m) ÷ drum radius (m). 10 N ≈ 1 kg of force.
- Car wiper motors: very roughly 3–6 N·m working, 15–30 N·m at stall. Measure yours.
- With a 40 mm drum (0.02 m radius) and 4 N·m: 200 N, about 20 kg of pull.
- Each layer of rope on the drum makes the radius bigger and the pull smaller.

Pulleys: a 2:1 block doubles the pull and halves the speed (less 10–20% friction). A 3:1 triples it.

Speed: rope speed (m/min) = drum circumference × rpm. A 40 mm drum at 40 rpm: about 5 m per minute.

## Motor options
| Motor | Volts | Speed | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| Car wiper | 12V | 40–70 rpm | Light pulls, holds when stopped |
| Power seat or window | 12V | slow | Light; small gears wear |
| Wheelchair or mobility scooter | 24V | 100–150 rpm | Strong; often has a parking brake |
| Cordless drill on low gear | 12–20V | 300–400 rpm | Fast, weak; clutch protects it |
| Ride-on toy gear motor | 6–12V | 100–300 rpm | Light |

A wheelchair motor's brake needs voltage to release. Wire the brake coil so it's powered only while the switch is pressed, and it will hold the load whenever you let go.

## Reversing with two relays
Each relay's common goes to one motor lead; normally-closed contacts to battery −, normally-open to battery +. Energise one relay to wind in, the other to pay out. Both off: the motor is shorted, which acts as a brake.

## Duty cycle
Small motors are rated for short runs. If the case gets too hot to touch, stop and let it cool. Don't hold a motor stalled.

## Rope or cable
Synthetic rope is lighter and stores less energy when it breaks, but chafes. Steel cable resists abrasion but whips badly and frays into sharp strands; wear gloves.

## Linear actuators
Power recliner and bed actuators push or pull 2,000–6,000 N over 100–300 mm. Not a winch, but excellent for short, strong pulls such as tensioning or lifting a hatch.

## If you lack a part
- No switch: two fused leads you touch to the battery, one pair each way. Crude; keep a hand on the fuse.
- No motor: a hand winch or a lever with a ratchet strap does the same job slowly.
